levels.name: Explorer
levels.summary: See how AI systems sense, decide, learn from examples, and stay under human direction.

blocks.text: Week 1: AI or Not?
Look for evidence of how the system reasons or learns, not just its label or screen.
EXPLORER MISSION Investigate, trace, test, and explain. Your independent proof: Sort six devices by mechanism and defend two borderline cases.
Explorer name:
Look Closely Before You Explain
Pictures give clues; evidence tells us what the clues mean.
MYSTERY A remote-control car, calculator, motion light, smart speaker, photo sorter, and robot vacuum may all look clever, but they do not make decisions in the same way.
What do you notice?
Name three visible details without explaining them yet.
Circle the detail most connected to the system's decision.
Name one detail that may be decoration or distraction.
Make a first prediction and state the clue that supports it.
My observations, prediction, and evidence:
GOOD THINKING A prediction can change when stronger evidence appears.
Input → Process → Output
Follow the information instead of imagining magic inside the machine.
INPUT a command, signal, photo, sound, or number
PROCESS a human choice, fixed instruction, or learned pattern
OUTPUT movement, calculation, action, or prediction
CORE IDEA Look for evidence of how the system reasons or learns, not just its label or screen.

UNDER THE HOOD A system should be classified by its decision mechanism. Human control, fixed automation, and model-based prediction can produce similar visible behavior, so appearance and marketing words are weak evidence.
Draw a fresh example with all three stages:
Four Cases, Four Clues
Use the visual cue, then read the evidence carefully.
CASE 1 — Remote car Clue: person sends each steering command. Meaning: human-controlled.
CASE 2 — Motion light Clue: written if-motion-then-light rule. Meaning: fixed automation.
CASE 3 — Photo sorter Clue: trained model predicts a new label. Meaning: AI-based.
CASE 4 — Robot vacuum Clue: description hides the mechanism. Meaning: not enough information.
BOUNDARY Do not call a system AI because it looks, moves, or talks like a person.
Which two pictures are easiest to confuse? What evidence separates them?
Words You Can See and Use
The badge is a memory cue; the definition does the real thinking work.

rows: a system using learned patterns or symbolic reasoning
a person makes the important choice
a clue that supports or changes a claim

blocks.text: Misconception detective
CLAIM TO REPAIR Every robot uses AI.
Use one vocabulary word and one piece of evidence to repair it:
WORD POWER A strong definition helps you decide something in a new case.
Watch the Reasoning, Not Just the Answer
Every step connects a claim to observable evidence.
CASE A remote-control car, calculator, motion light, smart speaker, photo sorter, and robot vacuum may all look clever, but they do not make decisions in the same way.
STEP 1 — OBSERVE a command, signal, photo, sound, or number
STEP 2 — TRACE a human choice, fixed instruction, or learned pattern
STEP 3 — CONCLUDE movement, calculation, action, or prediction

MODEL REASONING Follow the information and identify who or what makes the important choice. A robot body, screen, voice, or the word smart cannot prove AI. If two mechanisms fit the evidence, say that more information is needed.
DO NOT OVERCLAIM Do not call a system AI because it looks, moves, or talks like a person.
What new evidence could change this answer?
Same Result, Different Reason
A comparison helps reveal the true concept boundary.

rows: trained model predicts a new label

Climb from Recall to Defense
Each step asks for a stronger kind of understanding.
RECALL Define AI system.
EXPLAIN Look for evidence of how the system reasons or learns, not just its label or screen.

The situation
Six devices are a motion-triggered lamp, a trained photo sorter, a remote-controlled car, a calculator, an unspecified smart speaker and an unspecified robot vacuum.
The question
Classify all six using mechanism evidence. Which two need more information?
Worked explanation

The lamp uses a fixed rule; the photo sorter uses a learned model; the car follows human commands; the calculator performs arithmetic. The speaker and vacuum need mechanism details. Products can combine mechanisms. A robot body or smart label proves none of them.

blocks.text: Prepare the class

Use the supplied scenario, student illustrations and blank paper. For numeric work, offer counters or a calculator after learners show the setup. Fictional records are supplied; personal data and paid accounts are unnecessary.
Allow 80 minutes: recall 8; explanation 12; worked demonstration 15; guided practice 20; independent assessment 15; project and reflection 10. Extend the lab into a second session when needed.
Explain the mechanism
Follow the information instead of imagining magic inside the machine.
INPUT a command, signal, photo, sound, or number
PROCESS a human choice, fixed instruction, or learned pattern
OUTPUT movement, calculation, action, or prediction
CORE IDEA Look for evidence of how the system reasons or learns, not just its label or screen.

UNDER THE HOOD A system should be classified by its decision mechanism. Human control, fixed automation, and model-based prediction can produce similar visible behavior, so appearance and marketing words are weak evidence.

Every step connects a claim to observable evidence.

STEP 1 — OBSERVE a command, signal, photo, sound, or number
STEP 2 — TRACE a human choice, fixed instruction, or learned pattern
STEP 3 — CONCLUDE movement, calculation, action, or prediction

MODEL REASONING Follow the information and identify who or what makes the important choice. A robot body, screen, voice, or the word smart cannot prove AI. If two mechanisms fit the evidence, say that more information is needed.

Teacher precision note

This course concentrates on modern machine learning. AI also includes symbolic and rule-based approaches. A simple automatic switch or robot body is not, by itself, evidence of AI. Discuss how the system reasons or learns, rather than judging appearance.
Concrete teaching case
Six devices are a motion-triggered lamp, a trained photo sorter, a remote-controlled car, a calculator, an unspecified smart speaker and an unspecified robot vacuum.
Classify all six using mechanism evidence. Which two need more information?
Exact explanation to model

The lamp uses a fixed rule; the photo sorter uses a learned model; the car follows human commands; the calculator performs arithmetic. The speaker and vacuum need mechanism details. Products can combine mechanisms. A robot body or smart label proves none of them.
Demonstrate and guide practice
Board sequence
Write the given facts: Six devices are a motion-triggered lamp, a trained photo sorter, a remote-controlled car, a calculator, an unspecified smart speaker and an unspecified robot vacuum.
Write the question to explain: Classify all six using mechanism evidence. Which two need more information?

Reveal after predictions: The lamp uses a fixed rule; the photo sorter uses a learned model; the car follows human commands; the calculator performs arithmetic. The speaker and vacuum need mechanism details. Products can combine mechanisms. A robot body or smart label proves none of them.
Keep for an independent attempt: A thermostat follows a written temperature rule. Does its screen prove learning?
Classroom dialogue
Ask: Which facts are given, and which would we have to assume? Learners mark relevant details before discussing answers.
Say: Predict first. Show the rule, information path or calculation that would produce the result. A correct guess is not yet an explanation.
Reveal reasoning one step at a time. Explain why a tempting alternative fails. Write units and denominators for arithmetic, trace conditions for decisions, and identify supporting sources for claims.
In pairs, one learner solves while the other checks evidence; exchange roles. Remove the worked answer before independent assessment.
Run the weekly evidence lab
Predict first, test honestly, and explain what the evidence means.
State your prediction before the result is known.
Complete the task: Sort six devices by mechanism and defend two borderline cases.
Keep a normal case and an edge case clearly separated.
Record what happened—even when it does not match your prediction.
Explain the result, one limitation, and the next useful test.
INDEPENDENCE After support is removed, repeat the proof with a fresh case.
Make the lab runnable

Use the concrete case as the shared normal case and the independent question as a second case. Each pair creates a boundary or missing-information case and predicts its result before testing. Keep the expected result separate from an observed mistake.

blocks.text: Diagnose and reteach
CLAIM TO REPAIR Every robot uses AI.

For guessing, return to given facts and request a trace. For vocabulary without application, use one example and one non-example. For arithmetic errors, check the setup before the calculation. Finish with a different uncoached case before recording mastery.
Assess and explain the answers
Worked case answer

The lamp uses a fixed rule; the photo sorter uses a learned model; the car follows human commands; the calculator performs arithmetic. The speaker and vacuum need mechanism details. Products can combine mechanisms. A robot body or smart label proves none of them.
Independent question
A thermostat follows a written temperature rule. Does its screen prove learning?
Expected independent answer
No. Its stated mechanism is a fixed rule; appearance is insufficient evidence.
What counts as evidence

rows: Clear mechanism, calculation or source support

blocks.text: Use 6/8 as a classroom checkpoint, with 2 required for both Result and Reasoning. This is a proposed teaching rule, not a validated certification threshold. Do not count a coached answer as independent mastery; correct unsafe or unsupported claims regardless of total.
Feedback
Name the first missing reasoning step and ask for correction. Keep the first attempt and independent retry separate.
Connect and extend learning
Helpful Classroom Sorter
Choose whether the Helpful Classroom Sorter needs a person, fixed rule, or learned model; justify the smallest safe solution.
Keep the decision, input, result, explanation and remaining limitation in the project evidence record. Retrieve this record next week rather than restarting the project.
Support and stretch

Use physical cards, spoken explanations and a three-stage drawing. Read aloud without giving the answer. Stretch: compare two mechanisms with the same visible output and explain what evidence distinguishes them.
Exit reflection
Ask for one decision the learner can now justify and one situation requiring more evidence or human review. Confidence ratings are separate from correct independent performance.

Next: Week 2: Input, Process, Output. Retrieve today’s evidence and identify what carries forward and what is new.

Week 2: Input, Process, Output
A system transforms information; it does not simply 'know.'
EXPLORER MISSION Investigate, trace, test, and explain. Your independent proof: Trace a music recommender and draw all three stages.
Explorer name:
Look Closely Before You Explain
Pictures give clues; evidence tells us what the clues mean.
MYSTERY A music helper receives listening choices, compares them with a ranking process, and suggests a song. The suggestion appears only after information has moved through the system.
What do you notice?
Name three visible details without explaining them yet.
Circle the detail most connected to the system's decision.
Name one detail that may be decoration or distraction.
Make a first prediction and state the clue that supports it.
My observations, prediction, and evidence:
GOOD THINKING A prediction can change when stronger evidence appears.
Input → Process → Output
Follow the information instead of imagining magic inside the machine.
INPUT songs played, liked, or skipped
PROCESS compare clues and rank possible songs
OUTPUT a suggested song or a not-sure result
CORE IDEA A system transforms information; it does not simply 'know.'

UNDER THE HOOD Input, process, and output are functional roles. The process may contain human choices, fixed rules, calculations, retrieval, or a learned model. Naming the three stages prevents magical explanations of computer behavior.
Draw a fresh example with all three stages:
Four Cases, Four Clues
Use the visual cue, then read the evidence carefully.
CASE 1 — Camera app Clue: photo enters before any result. Meaning: input.
CASE 2 — Music ranking Clue: choices are compared and scored. Meaning: process.
CASE 3 — Song suggestion Clue: a result is shown to the user. Meaning: output.
CASE 4 — No listening history Clue: important input is missing. Meaning: not-sure case.
BOUNDARY The output is not proof that the system understood the input as a person would.
Which two pictures are easiest to confuse? What evidence separates them?
Words You Can See and Use
The badge is a memory cue; the definition does the real thinking work.

rows: the result produced by the system

Week 3: Sensors Are Messengers
Sensors measure signals; later processing gives those signals meaning.
EXPLORER MISSION Investigate, trace, test, and explain. Your independent proof: Match camera, microphone, and temperature sensors to data.
Explorer name:
Look Closely Before You Explain
Pictures give clues; evidence tells us what the clues mean.
MYSTERY A classroom weather station measures light, sound, and temperature but does not decide what those measurements mean.
What do you notice?
Name three visible details without explaining them yet.
Circle the detail most connected to the system's decision.
Name one detail that may be decoration or distraction.
Make a first prediction and state the clue that supports it.
My observations, prediction, and evidence:
GOOD THINKING A prediction can change when stronger evidence appears.
Input → Process → Output
Follow the information instead of imagining magic inside the machine.
INPUT light, sound, or heat from the environment
PROCESS a sensor converts the signal into recorded values

Allow 80 minutes: recall 8; explanation 12; worked demonstration 15; guided practice 20; independent assessment 15; project and reflection 10. Extend the lab into a second session when needed.
Explain the mechanism
Follow the information instead of imagining magic inside the machine.
INPUT goal, starting state, and available objects
PROCESS follow ordered unambiguous steps
OUTPUT completed task or a visible failure point
CORE IDEA An algorithm is an ordered, testable procedure, with or without code.

UNDER THE HOOD An algorithm is a finite procedure whose steps and control flow can be executed. Correctness depends on assumptions, preconditions, order, and termination. Code is one representation of an algorithm, not the definition itself.
Draw a fresh example with all three stages:
Every step connects a claim to observable evidence.
CASE A paper robot cannot infer missing intentions; it needs ordered steps that another person can execute and test.
STEP 1 — OBSERVE goal, starting state, and available objects
STEP 2 — TRACE follow ordered unambiguous steps
STEP 3 — CONCLUDE completed task or a visible failure point

MODEL REASONING A strong algorithm states the starting arrangement, names each object, orders actions, and includes checks such as whether the bag is open. The revision targets the failed assumption rather than replacing every step.
DO NOT OVERCLAIM A goal is not yet an algorithm; each step must tell the actor what to do.
What new evidence could change this answer?
Concrete teaching case
A robot starts on the left of three squares, facing right. It executes MOVE, MOVE, STOP, each MOVE being one square.
Trace the position after each command.
Exact explanation to model
Middle, rightmost, unchanged. Direction, distance and starting conditions must be specified.
Demonstrate and guide practice
Board sequence
Write the given facts: A robot starts on the left of three squares, facing right. It executes MOVE, MOVE, STOP, each MOVE being one square.
Write the question to explain: Trace the position after each command.
Reveal after predictions: Middle, rightmost, unchanged. Direction, distance and starting conditions must be specified.
Keep for an independent attempt: Start in the middle facing right and execute MOVE, STOP.
Classroom dialogue
Ask: Which facts are given, and which would we have to assume? Learners mark relevant details before discussing answers.
Say: Predict first. Show the rule, information path or calculation that would produce the result. A correct guess is not yet an explanation.
Reveal reasoning one step at a time. Explain why a tempting alternative fails. Write units and denominators for arithmetic, trace conditions for decisions, and identify supporting sources for claims.
In pairs, one learner solves while the other checks evidence; exchange roles. Remove the worked answer before independent assessment.
Run the weekly evidence lab
Predict first, test honestly, and explain what the evidence means.
State your prediction before the result is known.
Complete the task: Write directions for a paper robot to pack a bag.
Keep a normal case and an edge case clearly separated.
Record what happened—even when it does not match your prediction.
Explain the result, one limitation, and the next useful test.
INDEPENDENCE After support is removed, repeat the proof with a fresh case.
Make the lab runnable

Use the concrete case as the shared normal case and the independent question as a second case. Each pair creates a boundary or missing-information case and predicts its result before testing. Keep the expected result separate from an observed mistake.

Week 10: If/Then Decisions
Conditions make an algorithm branch when information changes.
EXPLORER MISSION Investigate, trace, test, and explain. Your independent proof: Build a weather-clothing rule and test four cases.
Explorer name:
Look Closely Before You Explain
Pictures give clues; evidence tells us what the clues mean.
MYSTERY A clothing helper follows different paths depending on temperature, rain, and wind conditions.
What do you notice?
Name three visible details without explaining them yet.
Circle the detail most connected to the system's decision.
Name one detail that may be decoration or distraction.
Make a first prediction and state the clue that supports it.
My observations, prediction, and evidence:
GOOD THINKING A prediction can change when stronger evidence appears.
Input → Process → Output
Follow the information instead of imagining magic inside the machine.
INPUT weather values
PROCESS check ordered if/then conditions
OUTPUT clothing suggestion and reason
CORE IDEA Conditions make an algorithm branch when information changes.

UNDER THE HOOD A conditional evaluates a Boolean expression and selects a branch. Order matters when conditions overlap. Complete decision logic needs explicit handling for boundary values and an else path.
Draw a fresh example with all three stages:
Four Cases, Four Clues
Use the visual cue, then read the evidence carefully.
CASE 1 — Rain = yes Clue: then choose raincoat. Meaning: clear binary branch.
CASE 2 — Temperature < 15 C Clue: then choose warm layer. Meaning: numeric threshold.
CASE 3 — Exactly 15 C Clue: needs boundary rule. Meaning: edge case.
CASE 4 — Rain and cold Clue: two conditions overlap. Meaning: order or combined rule needed.
BOUNDARY Never hide an unhandled case between two thresholds.
Which two pictures are easiest to confuse? What evidence separates them?

The badge is a memory cue; the definition does the real thinking work.

Week 11: Repeating Efficiently
A loop repeats a useful step until a stopping condition is met.
EXPLORER MISSION Investigate, trace, test, and explain. Your independent proof: Compress a repeated drawing algorithm using a loop card.
Explorer name:
Look Closely Before You Explain
Pictures give clues; evidence tells us what the clues mean.
MYSTERY Instead of writing draw-side and turn four times, a square algorithm can repeat those steps four times.
What do you notice?
Name three visible details without explaining them yet.
Circle the detail most connected to the system's decision.
Name one detail that may be decoration or distraction.
Make a first prediction and state the clue that supports it.
My observations, prediction, and evidence:
GOOD THINKING A prediction can change when stronger evidence appears.
Input → Process → Output
Follow the information instead of imagining magic inside the machine.
INPUT starting state and repeat count
PROCESS run the loop body and update progress
OUTPUT finished pattern when the stop condition is met
CORE IDEA A loop repeats a useful step until a stopping condition is met.

UNDER THE HOOD A loop requires an initialization, body, update, and termination condition. Repetition is safe only when each iteration moves state toward stopping; otherwise the loop may run forever or the wrong number of times.
Draw a fresh example with all three stages:
Four Cases, Four Clues
Use the visual cue, then read the evidence carefully.
CASE 1 — Square Clue: repeat move and turn 4 times. Meaning: counted loop.
CASE 2 — Pick cards Clue: repeat until pile empty. Meaning: condition loop.
CASE 3 — No counter update Clue: condition never changes. Meaning: infinite loop risk.
CASE 4 — Stop too early Clue: one item remains. Meaning: off-by-one error.
BOUNDARY Repeat forever is not an efficient algorithm unless endless operation is truly the goal and can be stopped safely.
Which two pictures are easiest to confuse? What evidence separates them?
Words You Can See and Use
The badge is a memory cue; the definition does the real thinking work.

MODEL REASONING Place only the repeated steps inside the loop, initialize the counter, update it once per pass, and stop after the required count. Trace each iteration to catch one-too-many or one-too-few errors.
DO NOT OVERCLAIM Repeat forever is not an efficient algorithm unless endless operation is truly the goal and can be stopped safely.

Debugging finds the broken assumption or step before changing the solution.

Explorer name:

Pictures give clues; evidence tells us what the clues mean.

What do you notice?
Name three visible details without explaining them yet.

My observations, prediction, and evidence:
GOOD THINKING A prediction can change when stronger evidence appears.
Input → Process → Output
Follow the information instead of imagining magic inside the machine.
INPUT expected path and actual trace
PROCESS locate the first difference and test one cause
OUTPUT targeted correction plus repeated test
CORE IDEA Debugging finds the broken assumption or step before changing the solution.

UNDER THE HOOD Debugging is causal diagnosis. The first observable divergence narrows the faulty assumption, data, state, condition, or step. Changing multiple things at once destroys evidence about which change repaired the behavior.
Draw a fresh example with all three stages:
Four Cases, Four Clues
Use the visual cue, then read the evidence carefully.
CASE 1 — Wrong turn Clue: first divergence at step 4. Meaning: inspect orientation assumption.
CASE 2 — Missing card Clue: input absent before step 1. Meaning: data/setup cause.
CASE 3 — Wrong threshold Clue: branch changes at 10. Meaning: condition cause.
CASE 4 — Random rewrite Clue: many steps changed. Meaning: weak debugging evidence.
BOUNDARY A successful new run does not prove the diagnosis if several things changed together.

CASE 4 — New dotted triangle Clue: unseen combination. Meaning: tests learned behavior.

Explain the mechanism

PROCESS rank possible outputs

Estimate slope and intercept from training pairs using least squares. Ages are weeks and heights are cm. Test targets are excluded from fitting; training ages must include distinct values.
n = len(train)
x_mean = sum(x for x, y in train) / n
y_mean = sum(y for x, y in train) / n
num = sum((x-x_mean)*(y-y_mean) for x, y in train)
den = sum((x-x_mean)**2 for x, y in train)
if den == 0:
raise ValueError('Distinct training ages required')
slope = num / den
intercept = y_mean - slope*x_mean
preds = [slope*x + intercept for x, y in test]
mae = sum(abs(y-pred) for pred, (x, y)
in zip(preds, test)) / len(test)
print(slope, intercept, preds, mae)

Allow 80 minutes: recall 8; explanation 12; worked demonstration 15; guided practice 20; independent assessment 15; project and reflection 10. Extend the lab into a second session when needed.
Explain the mechanism
Trace the information, fitted behavior, and evaluation proof separately.
QUESTION Compare simple and complex models using train and validation evidence.
MODEL IDEA An overfit model captures training-specific noise, producing a large gap between training and unseen performance.
PROOF NEEDED Use an unseen case, visible calculation, error analysis, and a stated limitation.
UNDER THE HOOD Simple tree: train 82%, validation 78%; gap 4 points. Deep tree: train 100%, validation 65%; gap 35 points.
Draw a fresh data → model → prediction → evaluation trace:
Predict first. Then check each step. A correct answer without visible evidence cannot be audited.
STEP 1 Simple tree: train 82%, validation 78%; gap 4 points.
STEP 2 Deep tree: train 100%, validation 65%; gap 35 points.
STEP 3 Deep tree's perfect training result is weaker unseen evidence.
STEP 4 Prune, regularize, improve representative data, or features—then rerun fixed validation cases.
CHECK Verify the denominator, unit, split, class definition, and data version before interpreting a score.
Recalculate, retrace, or restate the evidence independently:
Concrete teaching case
A scores100% train,60% validation; B scores85%,80% on the same sets.
Compute gaps and select by validation accuracy.
Exact explanation to model
A gap40 percentage points; B gap5. B has better shared validation accuracy. A suggests overfitting, but investigate distribution differences too.
Demonstrate and guide practice
Board sequence
Write the given facts: A scores100% train,60% validation; B scores85%,80% on the same sets.
Write the question to explain: Compute gaps and select by validation accuracy.
Reveal after predictions: A gap40 percentage points; B gap5. B has better shared validation accuracy. A suggests overfitting, but investigate distribution differences too.
Keep for an independent attempt: Can final test be reused repeatedly to choose A or B?
Classroom dialogue
Ask: Which facts are given, and which would we have to assume? Learners mark relevant details before discussing answers.
Say: Predict first. Show the rule, information path or calculation that would produce the result. A correct guess is not yet an explanation.
Reveal reasoning one step at a time. Explain why a tempting alternative fails. Write units and denominators for arithmetic, trace conditions for decisions, and identify supporting sources for claims.
In pairs, one learner solves while the other checks evidence; exchange roles. Remove the worked answer before independent assessment.
Run the weekly evidence lab
Keep the test conditions fixed, record every result, and change only one planned factor.
1. Write the hypothesis and expected evidence before running.
2. Complexity Trial: fit paper trees of increasing depth, plot train/validation results, and identify the first clear overfit pattern.
3. Run one normal, one boundary, one missing, and one shifted case.
4. Calculate the metric from raw counts or row-level errors.
5. Interpret what changed, what did not, and what remains unsafe or unknown.
Make the lab runnable

Use the concrete case as the shared normal case and the independent question as a second case. Each pair creates a boundary or missing-information case and predicts its result before testing. Keep the expected result separate from an observed mistake.

Builder name and experiment date:
Notice → Predict → Explain

Input → Model → Evidence
Trace the information, fitted behavior, and evaluation proof separately.
QUESTION Interpret three curve patterns and select a targeted next experiment.
MODEL IDEA Learning curves plot performance against training size or effort and help distinguish underfitting, overfitting, and data limitation.
PROOF NEEDED Use an unseen case, visible calculation, error analysis, and a stated limitation.
UNDER THE HOOD Both train and validation scores are low and close: likely underfitting. Train high, validation much lower: likely high variance or overfitting.
Draw a fresh data → model → prediction → evaluation trace:
Four Tests, Four Kinds of Evidence
A system is not understood until it survives more than one comfortable example.
NORMAL Expected data and expected behavior.
BOUNDARY Value close to a threshold, ambiguous label, or uncertain prediction.
MISSING Necessary field, label, source, or measurement is unavailable.
SHIFTED New lighting, species, device, subgroup, or time condition.
RELEASE RULE Passing one case never proves generalization. Predefine expected behavior for all four categories.
Which case most threatens today's claim, and why?
Words You Can Calculate and Defend
A definition matters when it lets you interpret a new dataset, model, or result.
MISCONCEPTION TO REPAIR Every learning curve that rises proves more data will solve the problem.
Repair the claim using a definition, calculation, or test record:
Reason Step by Step
Predict first. Then check each step. A correct answer without visible evidence cannot be audited.
STEP 1 Both train and validation scores are low and close: likely underfitting.
STEP 2 Train high, validation much lower: likely high variance or overfitting.
STEP 3 Validation improves as data grows and gap narrows: more representative data may help.
STEP 4 Curves suggest hypotheses; confirm with controlled experiments and error slices.
CHECK Verify the denominator, unit, split, class definition, and data version before interpreting a score.
Recalculate, retrace, or restate the evidence independently:
Compare → Diagnose → Repair
Do not patch the answer. Find the earliest unsupported assumption, data problem, or experiment error.
CLAIM TO CHALLENGE Every learning curve that rises proves more data will solve the problem.
Diagnose one cause and name the cleanest next experiment:
Specify Before You Run
A trustworthy result can be reproduced from the recorded data, code, settings, and evaluation rule.
Experiment record
QUESTION + intended use + success threshold
DATA version + grouped split + leakage check
CODE/preprocessing + features + model + settings + seed
METRICS + positive class + units + denominators
PREDICTIONS + errors + subgroup slices + limitations
HUMAN reviewer + release, revise, limit, or stop decision
Write the minimum record needed to reproduce today's result:
Predict → Run → Calculate → Interpret
Keep the test conditions fixed, record every result, and change only one planned factor.
1. Write the hypothesis and expected evidence before running.
2. Curve Clinic: match three graphs to diagnoses, challenge each diagnosis, and propose the smallest informative experiment.
3. Run one normal, one boundary, one missing, and one shifted case.
4. Calculate the metric from raw counts or row-level errors.
5. Interpret what changed, what did not, and what remains unsafe or unknown.
From Knowing the Word to Owning the Idea
Move upward only when you can produce evidence without copying the example.
DEFINE Use all four terms precisely: learning curve, bias, variance, plateau.
CALCULATE Reproduce the worked evidence with units and denominator.
TRACE Explain the data, code or decision path.
DIAGNOSE Every learning curve that rises proves more data will solve the problem.
TRANSFER Solve a fresh dataset or model case.
IMPROVE Change one cause and rerun fixed evidence.
DEFEND State intended use, metric, limitation, and human responsibility.
MASTERY RULE A coached calculation becomes mastery only after a different case is completed independently.

Support and stretch
Use a tiny labelled dataset, explicit units and a named positive class. Stretch: require a baseline, held-out evaluation and subgroup or shifted-condition analysis with denominators.
Exit reflection
Ask for one decision the learner can now justify and one situation requiring more evidence or human review. Confidence ratings are separate from correct independent performance.
Bridge to the next week
Review the full project evidence and choose concepts needing another independent attempt before the next level. One expo is not proof of mastery of all AI.
